objection: Didn’t Jesus say, ‘The Father is greater than I’—and call him the only true God?
answer:
Both texts you cite are real, and I won't soften them — but read in their full Gospel context, they describe the incarnate order of Persons, not a difference of nature.

John 14:28 comes from Jesus in the form of a servant, on His way to the cross, describing His mission from the Father who sent Him. The Fathers rightly distinguished statements Christ makes according to the economy of the incarnation from statements about His eternal essence. A son sent on a task can call the sender "greater" in respect of that mission's order without being of lesser nature — just as the Son's eternal relation to the Father as "begotten" implies an order of origin, not an inequality of being. That's why the same Gospel that records "the Father is greater than I" also opens by declaring the Word was God (John 1:1) and closes with Thomas confessing the risen Christ as "my Lord and my God" (John 20:28) — John is not contradicting himself.

John 17:3 is spoken in that same incarnate voice, in a prayer where Jesus has just asked the Father to glorify Him with the glory He had with the Father before the world existed — hardly the language of a mere creature. The verse distinguishes the Father and Son as persons; it doesn't exclude the Son from the divine identity any more than "my God and your God" in John 20:17 erases His divine sonship. There Christ is our God according to His eternal Word even while the Father is His God according to the humanity He assumed for our sake.

So the "one true God" language honors exactly what Trinitarian faith confesses: one God, known through the Father who sends and the Son who is sent — the Son not competing with the Father's deity but sharing it, as the Jews themselves understood when they charged Him with making Himself equal with God for calling God His own Father (John 5:17-18).

# The Witness Speaks

Look at John 14:28 plainly: *"The Father is greater than I."* Jesus says this himself—not a later theologian's inference, but his own words. And then in John 17:3, standing before his disciples at the end of his ministry, he defines eternal life as knowing "you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." If Jesus *is* God, how can he pray to the only true God and distinguish himself from that one God? The language is crystal clear: there is *one* God—the Father—and Jesus Christ is his Son. This isn't hostile to Jesus; it honors him as God's greatest creation and our Savior. But it respects what Scripture actually says about who the one true God is.

John 17:3 is spoken in that same incarnate voice, in a prayer where Jesus has just asked the Father to glorify Him with the glory He had with the Father before the world existed — hardly the language of a mere creature. The verse distinguishes the Father and Son as persons; it doesn't exclude the Son from the divine identity any more than "my God and your God" in John 20:17 erases His divine sonship. There Christ is our God according to His eternal Word even while the Father is His God according to the humanity He assumed for our sake.
